statement: In a meta-analysis of five placebo-controlled trials of bupropion or modafinil in people with methamphetamine dependence (642 participants), urine-verified abstinence in the final two weeks of treatment was about one in five with medication and with placebo (70 of 353, 19.8%, vs 62 of 289, 21.5%; OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.65–1.45; 5 fewer per 1,000, from 64 fewer to 69 more, the review's GRADE estimate from an assumed placebo rate of 215 per 1,000), with no significant difference between the two drugs in a subgroup test (p = 0.59). The five trials come from two investigator groups, two from one and three from the other, so they are not five independent replications. No dexamphetamine or methylphenidate trial entered this analysis, because none reported abstinence in a form the review could pool; of the six methylphenidate trials, four reported fewer positive urine tests than placebo on their own measures (for example OR 0.42, 0.24–0.72), two of them in people dependent on amphetamine rather than only methamphetamine, and two reported no difference. Across 14 trials of the four drugs, retention to the end of treatment was 53.0% vs 48.0% (OR 1.20, 0.91–1.58; 46 more per 1,000, from 23 fewer to 113 more, the review's estimate from an assumed placebo rate of 480 per 1,000).
plain: Pooling five trials, two medicines tested to help people stop using meth, bupropion and modafinil, did not lead to more people stopping than a placebo did: about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end of treatment in each group. The trials were small and uneven in quality, so a modest benefit or harm cannot be ruled out. Stimulant medicines such as dexamphetamine or methylphenidate were not part of this comparison; in the same review, four of six trials of methylphenidate reported fewer positive urine tests than a placebo, each measured in its own way, and two found no difference.
population: People with methamphetamine dependence in placebo-controlled trials (five trials for abstinence; 14 trials of amphetamine or methamphetamine use disorder for retention)
exposure: Bupropion or modafinil (abstinence); bupropion, modafinil, methylphenidate or dexamphetamine (retention)
outcome: Urine-verified abstinence in the last 2 weeks of treatment; retention to the end of the trial
magnitude: Abstinence 19.8% vs 21.5%, OR 0.97 (0.65–1.45), I² 2%; 5 fewer per 1,000 (64 fewer to 69 more). Retention 53.0% vs 48.0%, OR 1.20 (0.91–1.58), I² 15%; 46 more per 1,000 (23 fewer to 113 more) against an assumed placebo retention of 480 per 1,000.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials. Risk of bias: allocation concealment inadequately reported in more than three-quarters of trials, outcome assessment unclear or high risk in all, incomplete outcome data at high risk in half. Imprecision, two levels: the interval runs from about a third fewer to nearly half again as many abstinent people, so neither a useful benefit nor a harm is excluded, and only 132 people were abstinent. The review's own downgrade for inconsistency is not applied (I² 2% and 15%). Nor are its indirectness downgrades (serious for abstinence, for pooling different drugs and doses; very serious for retention, which also pooled populations that included people who inject drugs, incarcerated people and people with ADHD): the claim is worded to the pooled drugs, doses and populations and speaks for no single drug or dose, and the test between the two drugs for abstinence was not significant (p = 0.59). The five abstinence trials come from two investigator groups, so 'replicated' rests on two groups, not on five independent trials (METHODS §6.3). Very low certainty means the result cannot be read as showing that these drugs do not work.

evidence.extracted: Of the six methylphenidate trials, four reported a significant advantage over placebo on their own urine measures as tabulated by the review (Konstenius et al., 2014, drug-negative urines, p = 0.047; Ling et al., 2014, OR 0.18 for a positive urine at week 14, p = 0.025; Rezaei et al., 2015, fewer positive tests at week 10, p = 0.03; Tiihonen et al., 2007, OR 0.42, 0.24–0.72, p = 0.002) and two reported no difference (Konstenius et al., 2010; Miles et al., 2013). Konstenius et al. (2014) enrolled people with amphetamine dependence and Tiihonen et al. (2007) people with amphetamine or methamphetamine dependence. None entered the abstinence meta-analysis, from which trials were excluded when they lacked the information needed to count participants with sustained abstinence.
